name: Knowing What Students Know
title: Knowing What Students Know
answer: Knowing what students know is the starting point for any personalization, and AI can help teachers get there faster by sorting exit ticket responses into groups and flagging shaky earlier skills. The machine sorts and flags while the teacher interprets and decides, so AI saves time without taking over decisions about what each student does next.

sections.body: Personalized learning only works if the teacher knows where each student actually stands, and that knowledge has to be gathered constantly rather than assumed. Daily exit tickets, short questions at the end of a lesson, give a quick read on the class. AI can take those responses and sort them into groups such as students who got it, students sharing a common misconception, and students who need a fresh start. The teacher then checks the groupings and plans the next day. The idea solves the problem of personalization running on guesswork, replacing it with a fast, organized picture of student understanding.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher collects exit tickets through Google Forms and uses AI to sort the responses into groups, then reviews those groupings before planning the next lesson. Practice platforms add a second signal by flagging knowledge gaps, for example when a student keeps missing a certain kind of problem and the platform notes that an earlier skill is shaky. The teacher decides whether to go back and reteach that skill. The text does not give grade band variations, so the practice applies across levels: the routine is the same whether the exit ticket is a quick question or a short problem set, and the teacher remains the one who interprets the flag and chooses the response.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It describes the practice of using exit tickets and platform flags as a way to know where students stand, and it presents the division of labor between machine sorting and teacher judgment as a principle that runs through the Volume. This idea therefore rests on practice and professional reasoning rather than on research cited in the text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The flag from a practice platform is a lead to follow, not a diagnosis, and the teacher decides whether to go back and reteach a skill. AI sorts and flags, but the teacher interprets and acts, and that division of labor is especially important in personalized learning because decisions about what each student does next add up quickly. The limits are clear: the groupings and flags are inputs to teacher judgment, not conclusions, and the decisions about instruction stay with a person. Nothing in the text suggests handing those decisions to the machine.
